insider_note: Writing the numerator and denominator as (x−y)+3 and 2(x−y)+5 makes the coincident-ratio pattern visible at a glance, which is why the substitution here is x − y = v rather than any other combination.

steps.label: Test the coefficients and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Comparing coefficients shows a1/a2 = b1/b2 = 1/2, so x − y is the combination common to both.
steps.memory_tip: x − y + 3 and 2x − 2y + 5 are both built from x − y — that repeated block is the substitution.
lines: Comparing (x − y + 3)/(2x − 2y + 5) with (a1x + b1y + c1)/(a2x + b2y + c2)
So take the substitution x − y = v
steps.why: Both the numerator and denominator reduce to the same combination x − y with different constants added, which is exactly the coincident-ratio case, so treating x − y as a single new variable v collapses the equation to one unknown.
common_mistakes: Taking b1/b2 as −1/2 instead of correctly cancelling the two minus signs to get 1/2.
Choosing the substitution 2x − 2y = v instead of the simpler x − y = v.

steps.label: Reduce to a function of the new variable
steps.margin_note: One mark. Differentiate v = x − y to relate dv/dx to dy/dx, then substitute into (1).
steps.memory_tip: v = x − y gives dv/dx = 1 − dy/dx, so dy/dx = 1 − dv/dx.
lines: x − y = v ⇒ 1 − dy/dx = dv/dx ⇒ dy/dx = 1 − dv/dx
steps.why: Differentiating the substitution v = x − y gives a direct relation between dv/dx and dy/dx, which replaces dy/dx everywhere in (1) and leaves an equation purely in v and x.
common_mistakes: Writing dy/dx = dv/dx − 1 instead of 1 − dv/dx, a sign slip from differentiating x − y.
Substituting the un-simplified (x−y+3)/(2x−2y+5) instead of the rewritten (v+3)/(2v+5).

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Combine the two fractions on the right over the common denominator (2v + 5).
steps.memory_tip: (2v + 5) − (v + 3) = v + 2 — the numerator simplifies cleanly once the denominators match.
steps.why: Combining the two right-hand terms into a single fraction gives dv/dx as a clean function of v, and inverting turns the equation into a separated form ready for integration.
common_mistakes: Losing the +3 or the +5 when combining the two fractions.
Forgetting to invert dv/dx = (...) into dx = (...) dv before integrating.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Split (2v + 5)/(v + 2) into a whole number plus a simple fraction before integrating.
steps.memory_tip: 2v + 5 = 2(v + 2) + 1 — rewrite the numerator around the denominator's own bracket.
steps.why: Rewriting the top-heavy fraction as a constant plus a simple 1/(v+2) piece splits the integral into a plain term and a standard log term, which together give x as an explicit function of v.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate (2v + 5)/(v + 2) directly as a log without splitting off the constant 2 first.
Dropping the constant of integration c.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Substitute v = x − y and collect the x and y terms.
steps.memory_tip: x = 2v + log(v + 2) + c, with v = x − y, so 2v = 2x − 2y — watch the x terms combine on both sides.
lines: Putting v = x − y: x = 2(x − y) + log(x − y + 2) + c
steps.why: Substituting v = x − y returns the equation to the original variables, and collecting the x terms on one side gives the compact final relation the examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Combining x − 2x incorrectly and getting the sign of x wrong in the final line.
Leaving the constant on the wrong side, writing −x + 2y + log(x−y+2) = c instead of x − 2y + log(x−y+2) = c.
